content: 1. Bell et al. (United Kingdom, 2016–2018): This study evaluated the implementation of a postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) care bundle in 12 obstetric units, involving 15,660 women who experienced PPH after vaginal or cesarean delivery. The intervention included risk assessment, volumetric and gravimetric blood loss measurement, escalation of care to senior clinicians at specific blood loss thresholds (1,000 mL and 1,500 mL), point-of-care hemostasis testing with ROTEM-guided fibrinogen replacement, and tranexamic acid administration for abnormal bleeding. Compared to usual care (510 women), the intervention reduced severe PPH rates (≥2,500 mL) and transfusion requirements. However, data on other critical outcomes were insufficient, and the study had a high risk of bias. 2. Cho et al. (South Korea, 2007–2014): This before-and-after study assessed the SPEED protocol for PPH management in 229 women. The protocol included clinical assessment, emergency transfusion of O-positive red blood cells, and treatment plans based on vital signs and blood test results. Compared to usual care (74 women), the intervention showed insufficient data on critical outcomes. The study was rated as having a moderate risk of bias. 3. Colucci et al. (Switzerland, 2005–2012): A standardized management protocol for severe PPH was implemented in a single-center study involving 74 women. The protocol included uterine contraction stimulation, pharmacological measures (uterotonics, fluids, tranexamic acid), and emergency management (blood products, hemostatic agents, surgical procedures). Historical cohorts without standardized protocols were used as comparators. The intervention reduced estimated blood loss but had a high risk of bias and insufficient data on critical outcomes. 4. Escobar et al. (Colombia, 2011–2014): This study evaluated a PPH care bundle in 404 women, including the use of an obstetric Code Red team, non-pneumatic anti-shock garments, intrauterine Bakri balloons, hemostatic sutures, and institutional transfusion protocols. Compared to usual care (141 women), the intervention showed insufficient data on critical outcomes. The study had a high risk of bias. 5. Shields et al. (USA, 2011–2012): A patient safety initiative for PPH management was implemented in 29 maternity units, involving 21,602 women. The intervention included risk assessment, quantitative blood loss measurement, additional uterotonic doses, activation of multidisciplinary teams, and emergency release of blood products. Compared to usual care (10,433 women), the intervention showed insufficient data on critical outcomes and had a high risk of bias. 6. Skupski et al. (USA, 2000–2014): A hemorrhage management protocol was implemented for 44,782 women, including monitoring vital signs, diagnosing placenta previa/accreta, uterine massage, uterotonic agents, volume replacement, massive transfusion protocols, and surgical interventions. Compared to usual care (5,811 women), the intervention increased severe PPH rates (≥1,500 mL) and had insufficient data on other critical outcomes. The study had a critical risk of bias. 7. Main et al. (USA, 2011–2016): The CMQCC hemorrhage toolkit was implemented in 147 clusters, involving 9,821 women. The intervention included hemorrhage risk assessment, blood loss measurement, active management of the third stage of labor, and emergency blood product release protocols. Compared to usual care (48 clusters, 1,601 women), the intervention reduced severe maternal morbidity rates but had a high risk of bias. 8. Audureau et al. (France, 2002–2005): A regional multifaceted intervention for PPH prevention, diagnosis, and management was implemented in 19 maternity units, involving 35,386 women. The protocol included oxytocin administration, blood collection bags, manual removal of the placenta, intravenous sulprostone, and red blood cell transfusion. Compared to usual care (17,664 women), the intervention increased transfusion and hemostatic surgery rates but had insufficient data on other critical outcomes. The study had a moderate risk of bias. 9. Bingham et al. (USA, 2013–2016): The AWHONN PPH bundle was implemented in 58 hospitals, involving 2,852 health workers. The intervention included updated hemorrhage policies, blood loss quantification, risk assessments, and debriefing after hemorrhages. Insufficient data on critical outcomes were reported, and the study had a high risk of bias. 10. Chang et al. (Malawi, 2016–2017): A hemorrhage bundle was implemented in a central hospital and district health center, involving 2,694 women. The intervention included blood loss quantification, risk assessment tools, active management of the third stage of labor, standardized protocols, and simulation training. Compared to usual care (890 women), the intervention reduced maternal mortality rates from bleeding but had insufficient data on other critical outcomes. The study had a high risk of bias. 11. Davidson et al. (USA, 2018–2020): A quality improvement initiative was implemented for 13,659 women, including hemorrhage risk assessment, blood loss quantification, education on protocols, active management of the third stage of labor, and post-event debriefing. Compared to usual care (8,747 women), the intervention reduced severe maternal morbidity rates but had insufficient data on other critical outcomes. The study had a high risk of bias. 12. Duzyj et al. (USA, 2014–2018): The AWHONN PPH bundle was implemented for 2,297 women, including hemorrhage carts, massive transfusion protocols, active management of labor, and automated blood loss quantification. Compared to usual care (1,053 women), the intervention had insufficient data on critical outcomes and a high risk of bias. 13. Hamm et al. (USA, 2013–2015): A PPH bundle was implemented for 1,175 women, including standardized risk assessment tools, Bakri balloons, uterotonic medications, and hemorrhage response protocols. Compared to usual care (592 women), the intervention had insufficient data on critical outcomes and a critical risk of bias. 14. Seim et al. (Niger, 2012–2020): A PPH bundle was implemented in 8 regional hospitals, 35 district centers, and 1,217 peripheral health centers, involving 435,336 women. The intervention included misoprostol, intrauterine tamponade, and anti-shock garments. Compared to usual care (91,668 women), the intervention reduced maternal mortality rates but had a high risk of bias. 15. Sleutel et al. (USA, 2017–2020): An obstetric hemorrhage bundle was implemented in 9 hospitals, involving 18,520 women. The intervention included blood loss quantification, risk assessment, education, drills, and feedback mechanisms. Compared to usual care (9,272 women), the intervention reduced severe PPH rates (≥1,000 mL) but had insufficient data on other critical outcomes. The study had a high risk of bias. 16. Sullivan et al. (USA, 2017–2019): The CMQCC Obstetric Hemorrhage Toolkit was implemented for 6,735 women, including risk assessment, blood loss quantification, uterotonics, tranexamic acid, and activation of a PPH code. Compared to usual care (3,310 women), the intervention increased severe PPH rates (≥1,000 mL) and had insufficient data on other critical outcomes. The study had a high risk of bias.
